front: Visual metaphor: a toy shop manager can dispatch orders in three ways. Give each option, its goal, and the matching OS scheduling choice.
back:
• Dispatch orders immediately as they arrive (FIFO): low scheduling overhead; OS: first come first serve
  • Dispatch simple orders first: maximize orders processed over time, at the cost of assessing each order; OS: shortest job first (maximizes throughput)
  • Dispatch complex orders first: keep all workbench tools busy; OS: utilize all aspects of the platform (CPUs, devices, memory, other resources)

front: Scheduling: what does the CPU scheduler decide, and over which tasks?
back: It decides how and when processes and their threads access the shared CPUs. It schedules both user level and kernel level tasks.

front: Scheduling: name events that cause the scheduler to be run.
back:
• The CPU becomes idle (e.g. a task issues an I/O request and goes on a wait queue)
  • A timeslice expires
  • A new task becomes ready / enters the runqueue

front: Scheduling Overview: what is the scheduler's goal when it runs because the CPU went idle, and when it runs because a new task became ready?
back:
• CPU idle: select a task from the ready queue so the CPU is not idle for too long
  • New task ready: check whether the new task is of higher importance and should interrupt the currently executing task

front: Scheduling: once a task is selected, what steps dispatch it onto the CPU?
back: The OS context switches to the new task, enters user mode, sets the program counter, and execution begins.

front: Scheduling: what is the runqueue, and how is it related to the scheduling algorithm?
back: The runqueue is the structure of the ready queue. The runqueue and the scheduling algorithm are tightly coupled: a structure optimized for one algorithm may be a poor choice for another.

text: The two things that determine scheduler behavior are the scheduling {{c1::policy/algorithm}} (which task is selected) and the structure of the {{c2::runqueue}} (how the scheduler does its job).

front: Run To Completion scheduling: what is the core assumption?
back: Once a task is assigned to a CPU, it runs until it is finished (no interruption).

front: Run To Completion scheduling: list the four assumptions used for discussion.
back:
• A group of tasks need to be scheduled
  • We know the execution times of the tasks
  • There is no preemption
  • There is a single CPU

front: Scheduling: name common metrics used to compare schedulers.
back:
• Throughput
  • Average job completion time
  • Average job wait time
  • CPU utilization

front: FCFS: how does First Come First Serve schedule tasks, and what runqueue structure fits it?
back: Tasks are scheduled in the order they arrive; when a task completes, the next in order is picked. It fits a simple FIFO queue (enqueue at back, dequeue from front).

front: FCFS example (T1=1s, T2=10s, T3=1s, arriving in that order): throughput, average completion, average wait?
back:
• Throughput: 3 tasks / 12s = 0.25 tasks/sec
  • Average completion: (1 + 11 + 12)/3 = 8s
  • Average wait: (0 + 1 + 11)/3 = 4s
FCFS is simple, but its wait time is poor even with just one long task ahead of shorter tasks.

front: SJF: how does Shortest Job First order tasks, and what runqueue structures suit it?
back: It schedules jobs in order of execution time (shortest first); ties are broken arbitrarily. A FIFO queue no longer fits: use an ordered queue (costlier enqueue) or a tree ordered by execution time, where inserting may require rebalancing but selection is easy: the leftmost node has the smallest execution time.

front: SJF performance quiz (T1=1s, T2=10s, T3=1s, all in the system at time 0, no preemption, known execution times): execution order, throughput, average completion, average wait?
back:
Order: T1, T3, T2 (or T3, T1, T2).
  • Throughput: 3 tasks / 12s = 0.25 tasks/s (same as FCFS)
  • Average completion: (1 + 2 + 12)/3 = 5s (FCFS: 8s)
  • Average wait: (0 + 1 + 2)/3 = 1s (FCFS: 4s)

front: Preemptive SJF: which two Run-To-Completion assumptions are relaxed?
back:
• A task can now be interrupted (preempted) once started
  • Tasks no longer all arrive at the same time

front: Preemptive SJF: when T2 is running and shorter tasks T1/T3 arrive, what happens, and why must the scheduler run on arrival?
back: T2 is preempted in line with SJF. The scheduler must run whenever tasks enter the runqueue so it can inspect the new task's execution time and decide whether to preempt the current task.

front: Preemptive SJF: knowing execution time is unrealistic. How can the scheduler estimate it?
back: Use heuristics from past runs of the same task: how long the task took the last time, or a windowed average of execution times over the past n runs.

front: Preemptive SJF: why is assuming a known execution time unrealistic?
back: Execution time depends on many things outside the scheduler's view: the task's inputs, whether its data is present in the cache, and which other tasks are running.

front: Priority scheduling: what must the scheduler do, and what precondition does the policy require?
back: Run the highest priority task next. Precondition: the scheduler must be able to preempt lower priority tasks when a higher priority task enters the runqueue.

front: Priority scheduling: give the lecture's two examples of tasks with different priorities.
back:
• Kernel level tasks managing critical system components outrank tasks supporting user applications
  • Within a user-level process, threads that run on user input may outrank threads doing background processing for a long running simulation

front: Priority scheduling example: T2 runs alone, then T3 (highest priority) and T1 (lowest) become ready. What is the execution order, and when does T1 run?
back: T2 is preempted; T3 runs to completion, then T2 (higher than T1) runs to completion, then T1. T1 does not start until the 11th second and completes at time 12.

front: Priority scheduling: what runqueue structure lets the scheduler quickly tell a task's priority?
back: A separate runqueue per priority level, so the scheduler empties queues by priority level. Alternatively, an ordered structure like the SJF tree, but ordered by priority.

front: Priority scheduling: what is starvation?
back: A low priority task is essentially never scheduled because higher priority tasks continually enter the system and take precedence.

front: Priority scheduling: what is priority aging and how does it prevent starvation?
back: A task's effective priority becomes a function of its actual priority and the time it has spent in the runqueue. Older tasks are promoted to higher priority so they get scheduled in a reasonable time.

front: Preemptive priority quiz (P3 < P2 < P1): T3 arrives at 0 needing 4s, T2 at 3 needing 4s, T1 at 5 needing 3s. What are the finishing times?
back:
T3 runs 0-3; T2 preempts it and runs 3-5; T1 preempts T2 and runs 5-8; T2 runs its last 2s to 10; T3 runs its last 1s to 11.
T1 = 8s, T2 = 10s, T3 = 11s.

front: Priority inversion: define it using the T1/T2/T3 mutex scenario (P3 < P2 < P1).
back: The highest priority task (T1) ends up waiting on the lowest priority task (T3) which holds a needed mutex. The order should have been T1, T2, T3 but became T2, T3, T1.

front: Priority inversion: what is the solution, and what must the mutex data structure track for it?
back: Temporarily boost the mutex owner's priority to that of the waiting high priority task, then drop it back when the mutex is released. This requires tracking the current owner of the mutex in its data structure.

front: Round robin: how does basic round robin schedule equal-priority tasks?
back: Pick the task from the front of the queue and run it; when it completes (or yields), take the next task, cycling through the runqueue.

front: Round robin example: T1, T2, T3 are all in the runqueue; T1 blocks on I/O after one time unit. In what order do things run, and what if T1 did no I/O?
back: T1 runs 1 unit and yields for I/O; T2 runs to completion; T1's I/O completes and it rejoins the queue behind T3; T3 runs (two units); then T1 completes. Without the I/O the tasks simply run in queue order: T1, T2, T3.

front: Round robin: can it be combined with task priorities?
back: Yes. A higher priority arrival preempts the running lower priority task, and tasks of equal priority are scheduled round robin among themselves. Incorporating priorities requires preemption; without it, tasks are taken in FCFS order except that they may explicitly yield.

front: Round robin: what modification mixes in all tasks instead of waiting for each to yield?
back: Timeslicing: interrupt a task after a fixed window (e.g. one time unit) to schedule the next task, rather than waiting for it to explicitly yield.

front: Timeslice: define it (also called a time quantum).
back: The maximum amount of uninterrupted time that can be given to a task. A task may run less than this.

front: Timeslices: give reasons a task runs for less than its full timeslice.
back:
• It waits on an I/O operation
  • It synchronizes with another task
  • A higher priority task becomes runnable and preempts it

front: Timeslices: for which task type are they the only way to achieve timesharing, and why?
back: CPU bound tasks. I/O bound tasks are often placed on wait queues anyway, but CPU bound tasks only interleave via timeslices.

front: Timeslicing: what is the key benefit of round robin with timeslice=1 versus SJF regarding knowledge of execution times?
back: It matches SJF's average wait and completion without needing a priori knowledge of execution times (which is unfeasible in a real system).

front: Timeslicing example (T1=1s, T2=10s, T3=1s, all arriving at 0): give throughput, average wait, and average completion for RR with timeslice=1, and compare with SJF.
back: RR (ts=1): 0.25 tasks/s; wait (0 + 1 + 2)/3 = 1s; completion (1 + 12 + 3)/3 = 5.33s. On par with SJF (1s wait, 5s completion). Round robin without timeslices gives the FCFS metrics here, since these tasks do no I/O.

front: Timeslicing: list its benefits.
back:
• Short tasks finish sooner
  • Scheduler is more responsive to changes in the system
  • Lengthy I/O operations can be initiated sooner
E.g. an interactive T2 starts 1s in and can initiate its I/O then; under SJF it would start only after T1 and T3 complete.

front: Timeslicing: what is the downside, and what three steps make up its overhead?
back: The downside is overhead: (1) interrupt the running task, (2) execute the scheduler, (3) context switch to the new task.

front: Timeslicing: when only one runnable task remains, is overhead the same?
back: No. The timer still fires at timeslice intervals, but there is no scheduling or context switching (the dominant part of the overhead), so the overhead is much smaller.

front: Timeslicing: once its overhead is counted, what happens to throughput, average wait, and average completion?
back: Total time increases, so throughput goes down. Each task waits a little longer to start, so wait and completion times go up.

front: Timeslicing: what condition keeps context-switch overhead minimal?
back: The timeslice must be significantly longer than the time it takes to context switch.

front: Timeslice length: what single factor determines the right length, and does one answer fit all tasks?
back: The balance of timeslicing benefits against overheads. No single answer: it differs for I/O bound vs CPU bound tasks.
source: How Long Should a Timeslice Be

front: CPU bound timeslice: effect of a smaller timeslice on throughput/completion vs wait time?
back: Smaller timeslice means more frequent context switches, which degrades throughput and average completion, but tasks start sooner so average wait improves.

front: CPU bound tasks: do users care more about wait time or completion time, and what timeslice is best?
back: Users cannot perceive when a CPU bound task starts, so they care about completion, not wait. Prefer a larger timeslice; an infinite timeslice (never preempt) gives the best metrics.

front: CPU bound timeslice errata: for the 5-second timeslice (two 10s tasks, 0.1s switch), what is the correct average wait time?
back: 2.55 seconds, not 3.05. T1 starts at 0s and T2 starts at 5.1s, so wait = (0 + 5.1)/2 = 2.55; the lecture graphic has a division error listed in the course errata.

front: CPU bound timeslice example (two 10s tasks, 0.1s switch): compare the metrics for timeslice=1 vs timeslice=5.
back:
• ts=1: 0.091 tasks/s, wait 0.55s, completion 21.35s (T1 ends at 20.8s, T2 at 21.9s; the graphic says 20.85)
  • ts=5: 0.098 tasks/s, wait 2.55s, completion 17.75s
The larger timeslice wins on throughput and completion; the smaller one wins on wait.

front: I/O bound timeslice: with two I/O bound tasks that yield every 1s, why are timeslice=1 and timeslice=5 identical?
back: Each task yields the CPU after every second when it makes its I/O request, so there is essentially no preemption; the execution graphs and metrics are the same for both timeslices. They also match the CPU bound ts=1 case (average completion 21.35s; the graphic shows 20.85).

front: I/O bound timeslice (one I/O bound T2, one CPU bound T1): with timeslice=5, what goes wrong for T2's I/O?
back: T2's I/O latency can no longer be hidden: total execution time extends (throughput suffers) and T2 waits 5s for T1's timeslice to expire (average wait suffers). Average completion is lower only because of a large variance (T1 completes at about 11s, T2 much later); it is not an improvement for the I/O bound task.

front: I/O bound timeslice (T1 CPU bound, T2 I/O bound): how do the ts=1 and ts=5 schedules run?
back:
• ts=1: metrics unchanged; T1 is now explicitly preempted when its timeslice expires instead of yielding for I/O
  • ts=5: T1 runs until T=5; T2 runs 1s until its I/O request; T1 runs 5s more and completes; T2 then runs alone until it completes

front: I/O bound tasks: what timeslice length is preferred and what three things does it help?
back: A smaller timeslice. It keeps throughput up and average wait down, and maximizes device utilization by switching quickly between tasks issuing I/O requests.

text: CPU bound tasks prefer {{c1::longer}} timeslices (fewer context-switch overheads, high utilization/throughput), while I/O bound tasks prefer {{c2::shorter}} timeslices (issue I/O sooner, high device utilization, low wait).

front: Timeslice quiz (1 CPU, 10 I/O bound tasks issuing I/O after every 1ms of CPU, I/O takes 10ms, 1 CPU bound task, 0.1ms context switch): CPU utilization with RR at a 1ms and a 10ms timeslice?
back:
Utilization = useful CPU time / (useful time + context switch overhead).
  • 1ms: every 1ms of useful work costs 1.1ms, so 1/1.1 = 91%
  • 10ms: the 10 I/O tasks run 1ms each, then the CPU bound task runs 10ms: (10 x 1 + 10)/(10 x 1.1 + 10.1) = 20/21.1 = 95%

front: Timeslice quiz: which timeslice is better for CPU utilization and which for the I/O device, and why?
back: The large (10ms) timeslice, which favors the CPU bound task, gives better CPU utilization. A smaller timeslice is better for the I/O device, which cannot do anything while the CPU bound task runs its full 10ms.

front: Runqueue data structure: is it literally a queue, and what is the one requirement?
back: Only logically a queue; it may be multiple queues or a tree. The one requirement is that the scheduler can easily determine the next task to schedule. E.g. to give I/O and CPU bound tasks different timeslices, use one runqueue where the scheduler checks the task type, or separate runqueues.

front: Runqueue: describe the multi-queue structure for mixed I/O and CPU bound tasks.
back: Multiple distinct queues differentiated by timeslice value: I/O intensive tasks go in the queue with the smallest timeslices, CPU intensive tasks go in the queue with the largest timeslices.

front: Multi-queue runqueue example: what timeslice does each of the three queues get, and which queue does the scheduler check first?
back:
• Most I/O intensive: 8 ms
  • Mix of I/O and CPU: 16 ms
  • CPU intensive: infinite (effectively FCFS)
The I/O intensive queue has the highest priority and is checked first; the CPU bound queue is checked last.

front: Runqueue: why is the multi-queue (by timeslice) structure beneficial?
back: It provides timeslicing benefits for I/O bound tasks while avoiding timeslicing overheads for CPU bound tasks.

front: Runqueue: why are history-based heuristics alone not enough to tell whether a task is CPU or I/O bound?
back: They do not help with new tasks or tasks with dynamic behavior. So the scheduler must move tasks between queues (which leads to the MLFQ).

front: MLFQ: where is a new task placed, and what happens if it yields before its timeslice expires?
back: A new task goes on the topmost queue (lowest timeslice), as if it were the most demanding task in terms of scheduling operations. If it yields before the timeslice expires, that was a good choice; it returns to the same queue when runnable again.

front: MLFQ: what happens when a task has to be preempted, and when does the scheduler move it back up?
back: Being preempted implies it is more CPU intensive than thought, so it is pushed down to a longer-timeslice queue (possibly to the bottom). If a lower-queue task begins frequently releasing the CPU on I/O waits, the scheduler boosts it to a smaller-timeslice queue.

front: MLFQ: how does it differ from a plain group of priority queues?
back: Each level has different scheduling policies, and the structure provides feedback on a task so the scheduler learns over time which queue a task belongs to.

front: MLFQ history: who is credited and which production scheduler is essentially an MLFQ?
back: Fernando Corbato received the Turing Award in part for the MLFQ and timesharing work. The Solaris scheduler is essentially an MLFQ with 60 levels and its own feedback rules.

front: Linux O(1) scheduler: where does the name come from, and what type of scheduler is it?
back: It can add/select a task in constant time regardless of the number of tasks. It is a preemptive, priority-based scheduler.

front: Linux O(1): how many priority levels, and how are they split?
back: 140 levels, 0 highest and 139 lowest: 0 to 99 for real-time tasks and 100 to 139 for timesharing tasks.

front: Linux O(1): what is the default user process priority, and what are nice values?
back: Default timesharing priority is 120 (middle). Nice values span -20 to 19 (120-20 to 120+19) and are set via a system call.

front: Linux O(1): what feedback signal does it use, and how does it change priority?
back: How long the task spent sleeping (idling/waiting) during its timeslice. More sleeping means more interactive, so priority is boosted (priority - 5); less sleeping means more compute-intensive, so priority is lowered (priority + 5, up to a maximum).

front: Linux O(1): how is the runqueue implemented, and what are the two arrays called?
back: As two arrays of tasks, each element pointing to the first runnable task at that priority level. The arrays are active and expired.

front: Linux O(1): why does selecting a task take constant time?
back: The scheduler uses instructions that return the first set bit in a bit sequence (one bit per priority level, set means tasks present), then indexes into the array and takes the first task; all constant time.

front: Linux O(1): why does adding a task take constant time?
back: It takes constant time to index into the array by priority and then follow the pointer to the end of that level's task list to enqueue the task.

front: Linux O(1): what two ideas does it borrow from the MLFQ?
back:
• Each priority level has a different timeslice value (smallest for low-priority CPU bound tasks, largest for interactive tasks)
  • It uses feedback from how tasks behaved in the past to prioritize them in the future

front: Linux O(1): when does a task go to the active array vs the expired array, and what happens when active empties?
back: If it used less than its timeslice (yielded or preempted), it returns to the active queue. Only after exhausting its full timeslice does it move to expired. When active is empty, the active and expired arrays are swapped.

front: Linux O(1): why do the lowest priority tasks get the smallest timeslices?
back: Low priority tasks only run after all higher priority tasks expire; giving them small timeslices ensures they do not block higher priority tasks for too long: they get a small window, then quickly yield back.

front: Linux O(1): how do the active and expired arrays act as an aging mechanism?
back: High priority tasks eventually consume their timeslices and move to the expired array, at which point the low priority tasks get a chance to run for their small timeslices.

front: Linux O(1): when was it introduced, why was it replaced, and by what?
back: Introduced in Linux 2.5 by Ingo Molnar. It significantly hurt interactive tasks: as applications became more time sensitive (Skype, movie streaming, gaming), its jitter became unacceptable. It was replaced by the Completely Fair Scheduler (CFS) in Linux 2.6.23.

front: Linux O(1) vs CFS: who developed each, and can a Linux system still switch back to the O(1) scheduler?
back: Both were developed by the same person, and both are part of the standard Linux distribution, so it is possible to switch back to the O(1) scheduler (CFS is the default).

front: CFS motivation: what problem with the O(1) expired queue hurts interactive tasks?
back: Once a task enters the expired queue, it cannot run again until all other active tasks have run their timeslices, introducing jitter into interactions that should be seamless.

front: CFS: define fairness as the scheduler should guarantee it.
back: In a given time interval, a task should be able to run for an amount of time proportional to its priority. There are multiple formal definitions of fairness.

front: CFS: which Linux tasks does it schedule by default, and which does it not?
back: It is the default scheduler for non-realtime tasks; realtime tasks are scheduled by a realtime scheduler.

front: CFS: what runqueue data structure does it use and what property does it have?
back: A red-black tree, a self-balancing tree where all paths from root to leaves are approximately the same length.

front: CFS: what is vruntime and how are tasks ordered by it in the tree?
back: vruntime (virtual runtime) is the amount of time a task has spent running on the CPU, tracked to the nanosecond. Nodes to the left have lower vruntime (scheduled sooner); nodes to the right have larger vruntime (can wait). Each internal node is a task; the leaves play no role.

front: CFS: which node does it schedule, and how does it decide whether to preempt the running task?
back: It schedules the node with the least vruntime (typically the leftmost). It periodically increments the running task's vruntime and compares to the leftmost node's; if the running task's vruntime is still smaller it keeps running, otherwise it is preempted and reinserted.

front: CFS: how does the rate at which vruntime progresses differ by priority?
back: CFS changes the effective rate at which vruntime progresses. Lower priority: time passes more quickly, vruntime progresses faster, so the task likely loses the CPU sooner. Higher priority: vruntime progresses slower, so the task executes on the CPU longer.

front: CFS vs O(1): how many runqueue structures does CFS use across priority levels?
back: One runqueue (the red-black tree) for all priority levels, unlike the per-priority queues of the O(1) scheduler.

front: CFS: what are the time complexities of selecting a task and adding a task?
back: Selecting takes constant time (leftmost node); adding takes log(n) time relative to the total number of tasks. At typical current loads, log(n) is acceptable.

front: CFS: what is the potential future limitation of its log(n) add step?
back: As the number of tasks grows past a threshold, the log(n) add may limit the scheduler, prompting a search for a fair scheduler that can both select and add in constant time.

front: Linux schedulers quiz: what was the main reason O(1) was replaced by CFS? Judge: (a) scheduling under high load took unpredictable time, (b) low priority tasks could starve, (c) interactive tasks could wait unpredictable amounts of time.
back:
• (a) Incorrect: O(1) selects and schedules a task in constant time regardless of load
  • (b) Sort of correct: low priority tasks could wait unpredictably, possibly indefinitely, but this was not the main reason
  • (c) Correct: workloads became more interactive and demanded predictability, but a task in the expired array had to wait until the active array's tasks used up their timeslices

front: Linux schedulers: why did Linus Torvalds long resist a scheduler for small interactive tasks, and what changed?
back: Linux was a general purpose operating system. As general purpose workloads themselves changed (became more interactive), Linux needed a scheduler that met those needs, and CFS did.

front: Multiprocessor architecture: describe a shared memory multiprocessor's cache/memory layout.
back: Multiple CPUs, each with its own private L1/L2 cache, a last-level cache (LLC) that may or may not be shared, and shared system memory (DRAM).

front: Multiprocessor architecture: how does a multicore system differ in cache layout?
back: Each CPU has multiple internal cores; each core has its own private L1/L2, and the whole CPU shares an LLC, with DRAM present. Dual-core CPUs are common in laptops and phones; servers commonly have multiple CPUs with 6 or 8 cores each.

front: Multiprocessor scheduling: what is cache affinity and why does it matter?
back: Scheduling a task back on the same CPU it ran on before, to keep that CPU's cache hot. Performance depends heavily on execution state being in cache rather than main memory.

front: Multiprocessor scheduling: what architecture achieves cache affinity?
back: A hierarchical scheduling architecture: a load balancing component divides tasks among CPUs, and each CPU has its own scheduler and runqueue scheduling only its own tasks.

front: Multiprocessor scheduling: how is load balanced across CPUs?
back: Compare the lengths of the runqueues so one is not much longer than another, and detect idle CPUs to rebalance work from busier queues onto the idle CPU's queue.

front: NUMA: what defines a non-uniform memory access platform?
back: Multiple memory nodes connected to CPUs via an interconnect (e.g. Intel QuickPath Interconnect, QPI), where a memory node is closer to one socket, making local access faster than remote access.

front: NUMA-aware scheduling: what is the scheduling goal on a NUMA platform?
back: Keep tasks on the CPU closest to the memory node holding their state, to maximize memory access speed.

front: Hyperthreading: why do we have to context switch among threads in the first place?
back: Because the CPU normally has only one set of registers to describe an execution context.

front: Hyperthreading: what hardware feature enables it?
back: CPUs with multiple sets of registers, each set describing the context of a separate thread.

front: Hyperthreading: how many threads execute at once, and what is fast about it?
back: Only one thread executes at a given time (still one CPU), but context switching among the threads is very fast because each has hardware-supported context.

text: Hyperthreading goes by several names: hardware multithreading, hyperthreading, {{c1::chip multithreading (CMT)}}, and {{c2::simultaneous multithreading (SMT)}}.

front: Hyperthreading: how many hardware threads do modern platforms support, and can it be toggled?
back: Often two, with some high performance platforms up to eight. It can be enabled/disabled at boot time due to tradeoffs.

front: Scheduling: on a multicore system with hyperthreading enabled, what does the OS see as entities onto which it can schedule tasks?
back: Every CPU, every core in each CPU, and every hardware context.

front: Hyperthreading: why can it hide memory access latency?
back: A hardware context switch takes on the order of cycles, while a DRAM access takes hundreds of cycles, so switching hardware threads while one waits on memory is worthwhile: hyperthreading can hide memory access latency.

front: Hyperthreading scheduling: list the modeling assumptions used.
back:
• A thread can issue an instruction every CPU cycle (CPU bound maximizes IPC)
  • Memory access takes 4 cycles (memory bound thread idles while waiting)
  • Hardware switching is instantaneous
  • SMT platform with two hardware threads

front: Hyperthreading: what happens when co-scheduling two compute-bound threads?
back: Only one can issue per cycle (single pipeline), so they contend for pipeline resources; best case each idles every other cycle, so each thread's performance degrades by a factor of two and memory sits idle.

front: Hyperthreading: what happens when co-scheduling two memory-bound threads?
back: Both threads spend idle time waiting on memory access to return, resulting in wasted CPU cycles.

front: Hyperthreading: why is co-scheduling a mix of CPU and memory-bound threads best?
back: Run the CPU-bound thread until the memory-bound thread needs to issue a request, switch over to issue it, then switch back. This minimizes wasted CPU cycles and keeps both CPU and memory utilized, with only minimal interference. Some degradation remains: the compute-bound thread executes only three of every four cycles compared to running alone.

front: Paper (Fedorova et al.): the lecture uses a two-hardware-thread picture. What three-system comparison does the paper use instead?
back:
• A: single-threaded core (lower bound)
  • B: multithreaded core
  • C: multiprocessor with one core per thread (upper bound)

front: Paper (Fedorova et al.): in the A/B/C comparison, how do the systems perform on purely CPU-bound vs purely memory-bound workloads?
back: On a CPU-bound workload, A and B perform comparably while C is four times faster. On a memory-bound workload, B and C both beat A by a factor of four, because the multithreaded core overlaps the four threads' memory latencies.

front: Paper (Fedorova et al.): what instruction delay latencies ground the contention argument?
back: An ALU instruction has 0 delay latency, an L1-cache-hit load has 4 cycles, and a branch delays the next instruction by 2 cycles.

front: Paper (Fedorova et al.): what is the paper's headline result for a CMT-aware scheduler?
back: A CMT-aware scheduler can improve application performance by as much as a factor of two over a naive one.

front: CPU vs memory bound: why can't the sleep-time approach (used for interactive vs CPU intensive) be reused here?
back:
• A thread waiting on memory is not really sleeping; it waits in the processor pipeline, not on a software queue
  • Tracking sleep time used software methods, which are too slow given context switches on the order of cycles

front: CPU vs memory bound: what hardware mechanism helps, and what do they track?
back: Hardware counters, updated as the processor executes. They track things like L1/L2/LLC cache misses, the number of instructions retired (from which IPC can be computed), and power/energy usage. Counters are not uniform across platforms (the oprofile website lists them per architecture).

front: CPU vs memory bound: name software interfaces for accessing hardware counters.
back:
• oprofile
  • Linux perf tool

front: CPU vs memory bound: how does a scheduler use hardware counters to make decisions?
back: It uses counter data about a thread's resource needs to pick a good mix of threads from the runqueue so all system components are well utilized and threads interfere with each other as little as possible.

front: Hardware counters: a thread shows many LLC misses. Why is that not conclusive, and how do schedulers cope?
back: It may be memory bound (footprint does not fit in the cache), or it may have entered a new execution phase with a cold cache. One counter can mean different things, so schedulers guesstimate: they combine multiple counters and use platform-specific models trained on well-understood workloads.

front: Scheduling with hardware counters: what metric does Fedorova propose, and how does CPI differ for memory-bound vs CPU-bound threads?
back: Cycles Per Instruction (CPI). A memory bound thread has a high CPI (many cycles per instruction); a CPU bound thread has a CPI of 1 or some low number.

front: Paper (Fedorova et al.): the lecture says Fedorova merely "speculates" that CPI helps. How does the paper actually frame mean CPI?
back: The paper is less tentative: Section 5 states that mean CPI, easily determined using hardware counters, gives a useful window into the dynamic instruction mix of a workload and nicely captures average instruction delay.

front: Paper (Fedorova et al.): what does the paper's single-threaded CPI reasoning say a high vs low CPI implies?
back: A high single-threaded CPI means the thread spends much time blocked on memory or long-latency instructions, so it has low pipeline resource requirements; a low CPI means high resource requirements. The lecture's "high CPI implies memory bound" is the same idea stated via behavior rather than resource demand.

front: Paper (Fedorova et al.): what is single-threaded CPI?
back: The CPI a thread would show if it ran on a dedicated processor.

front: Scheduling with hardware counters: why does Fedorova use a simulator for the CPI study?
back: There is no CPI counter on her processor, and computing something like 1 / IPC would require unacceptable software intervention, so she uses a simulator in which the CPU is assumed to have a CPI counter. Her hope: if CPI proves useful, hardware engineers will add this counter to future architectures.

front: Scheduling with hardware counters: describe the simulated system and the synthetic workload's CPI values.
back: 4 cores, each with 4-way SMT, for 16 hardware execution contexts. Synthetic threads have CPI of 1, 6, 11, 16 (CPI 1 most CPU-intensive, CPI 16 most memory-intensive), four threads of each kind.

front: Fedorova CPI experiment: how are threads assigned to cores in experiments (a) and (d)?
back: Assignments are manual and static, mimicking a scheduler's decisions. (a): every core runs the identical mix of CPI 1, 6, 11, 16. (d): very different mixes per core, e.g. core 0 all CPI 1, core 3 all CPI 16. (b) and (c) fall between these extremes.

front: Scheduling with hardware counters: what metric assesses performance and what is its maximum here?
back: IPC is the metric; since the max number of cores is 4, the maximum IPC is 4.

front: Paper (Fedorova et al.): the lecture calls the simulated platform SMT. What core does the paper actually model?
back: Fine-grained multithreading (Laudon et al.), not SMT: one set of functional units, switching context every cycle, so at most one instruction issues per cycle and per-core IPC maxes at 1. The paper names SMT as the design it deliberately did not take, choosing a simple RISC core to fit more cores on the chip.

front: CPI experiment results: how do balanced-mix cores (experiments a, b) compare to similar-CPI cores (c, d)?
back: Balanced mixes utilize the pipeline well and give high IPC (not the maximum of 4, but fairly high). Cores with similar/identical CPI (c, d) are poorly utilized: CPU bound tasks contend, memory bound tasks leave the CPU idling, so IPC drops significantly. Cores 0 and 1 (mostly low-CPI tasks) contend for the pipeline, while cores 2 and 3 (mostly memory intensive) contribute very little to aggregate IPC.

front: CPI experiment results: what is the overall conclusion about CPI mix and utilization?
back: Scheduling tasks with mixed CPI values leads to higher platform utilization.

front: Paper (Fedorova et al.): what magnitudes does Section 5 give for the good vs poor schedules?
back: Schedules (a) and (b) perform twice as well as (d) and 1.5 times better than (c). In the poor schedules the CPI-1 threads are packed together (two cores of 1, 1, 6, 6 in (c); one core of 1, 1, 1, 1 in (d)), so those cores are saturated while the cores holding only high-CPI (memory-bound) threads are under-utilized.

front: CPI experiment results: when Fedorova profiled real benchmark applications, what did the CPI values look like?
back: They were cluttered together, not distinct like the synthetic workload; most CPIs ranged from 2.5 to 4.5 (per the lecture graphic).

front: CPI experiment results: what is the lecture's takeaway about CPI as a scheduling metric from the real profiling?
back: Because CPI is not that different across applications, it may not be the most instructive metric for scheduling decisions.

front: Paper (Fedorova et al.): the lecture concludes CPIs cluster so CPI is not useful. What does the paper actually conclude from its profiling?
back: The opposite: Section 5 reports measured CPI can vary by an order of magnitude among applications and that near-term CPI is predictable, so constructing a scheduler that balances load across CPU cores on a CMT processor should be a simple matter of engineering. The paper never gives a "2.5 to 4.5" range (that is the lecture graphic).

front: Paper (Fedorova et al.): what are the paper's own stated limitations of CPI, and what does her later work blame instead?
back: CPI does not reveal which specific resources (cache hierarchy, FPU) threads contend for, and CPI measured on a busy system is already perturbed by existing contention. Her later work (USENIX 2005) identifies L2 cache contention, not pipeline CPI, as the dominant effect.

front: CPI experiment results: even though the paper's CPI approach does not work in practice, what are the lecture's three takeaways?
back:
• SMT platforms have resource contention issues, here with the processor pipeline as the resource
  • Hardware counters can characterize a workload and inform OS-level resource management
  • Schedulers should consider resource contention, not just load balancing: pick tasks that will not contend for the pipeline, the cache, the memory controller, or an I/O device

front: Follow-on work to Fedorova: which resource is a particularly important contributor to degradation on hardware multithreaded or multicore platforms, and what should the scheduler do?
back: The cache, in particular the last level cache (LLC). The scheduler should track how a set of threads uses the cache and pick a mix that does not cause contention on the LLC.
